standard.title: Pi and Circle Features
standard.description: describe the relationship between π and the features of circles including the circumference, radius and diameter
standard.prior_knowledge: Students are familiar with circle vocabulary (centre, radius, diameter) from informal prior experience. Students can measure length and calculate with decimals (from AC9M6M01, AC9M7N06).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe π as the constant ratio of circumference to diameter and use this relationship to calculate circumference and diameter.

nodes.label: Features of circles and their relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and name the features of a circle (radius, diameter, circumference, chord) and state that diameter = 2 × radius.
nodes.minimum_width: Label all features on a circle diagram; state the relationship between radius and diameter.
nodes.typical_width: Measure radius and diameter of several circles; verify d = 2r consistently; identify chord, arc, sector informally.
wider: Investigate circles in First Nations Australian contexts: circular designs in weaving, significance of circles in cultural practices.
Explore how changing the radius changes both the diameter and circumference proportionally.

response_modes.reason: Circle vocabulary and the d = 2r relationship must be automatic before investigating π. Students who confuse radius and diameter make systematic errors in all circle calculations.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who confuse radius and diameter use the wrong measurement when calculating C/d in Node 2, making π appear to be approximately 6.28 or 1.57 — this completely undermines the discovery of π's constancy and all subsequent circumference calculations.
success_criteria: Correctly identifies and labels all key features of a circle.
States that diameter = 2 × radius and applies it correctly.
Does not confuse radius with diameter.

nodes.label: Discovering π as a constant ratio
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students investigate the ratio C/d for multiple circles and recognise that it is always approximately 3.14 — this constant is π.
nodes.minimum_width: Measure the circumference and diameter of at least two circles; calculate C/d and observe the approximate constancy.
nodes.typical_width: Calculate C/d for several circles with different sizes; record results; discuss why the ratio is constant; state that this constant is named π.
wider: Investigate the history of π and how mathematicians approximated it using polygons.
Explore why π is irrational — it cannot be written as an exact fraction, only approximated.

response_modes.reason: The constancy of C/d is not obvious from a single measurement. Multiple circles of very different sizes make the invariance of π compelling rather than arbitrary.

success_criteria: Measures and calculates C/d for at least two circles and observes the result is approximately 3.14.
States that π ≈ 3.14 and explains what it represents.
Does not treat π as just a button on a calculator without understanding its meaning.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The history and irrationality of π, and its emergence from measurement, is conceptually rich for advancing students — it connects the procedural formula to a deep mathematical idea.

nodes.label: Using π to calculate circumference and diameter
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use C = πd (or C = 2πr) to calculate the circumference given the diameter or radius, and rearrange to find diameter given circumference.
nodes.minimum_width: Calculate the circumference of a circle given its diameter or radius; find the diameter given the circumference.
nodes.typical_width: Solve practical problems involving circumference: wheel rotations, perimeter of semicircles, circular paths.
wider: Investigate how many rotations a wheel of a given diameter makes over a set distance.
Explore applications of circumference in First Nations contexts: circular fish traps, traditional circular dwelling dimensions.

response_modes.reason: Students need varied practical contexts to understand when C = πd is the right tool. Purely procedural practice leads to application failures in novel problems.

success_criteria: Correctly calculates circumference given diameter or radius.
Uses an appropriate approximation for π and specifies it.
